stem: Several weeks after acute pancreatitis, a client has persistent upper-abdominal pain and a newly palpable abdominal mass. Which complication should the nurse suspect?

options.A: Uncomplicated resolution of pancreatitis, because a new palpable abdominal mass is an expected recovery finding.
options.B: Renal colic, because a pancreatic complication would not persist or develop several weeks after acute pancreatitis.
options.C: Acute appendicitis, because post-pancreatitis pancreatic fluid collections do not cause persistent upper-abdominal symptoms.
options.D: A pancreatic pseudocyst or other post-pancreatitis pancreatic fluid collection requiring further evaluation.

rationale: Current StatPearls guidance states that pancreatic pseudocysts commonly arise after acute or chronic pancreatitis and generally mature more than 4 weeks after the onset of pancreatitis. Persistent abdominal pain and a new palpable abdominal mass after pancreatitis are clinical features that should raise suspicion for a pseudocyst or related pancreatic fluid collection and prompt imaging/evaluation. Therefore D is correct. A falsely treats a new mass as expected recovery, B incorrectly excludes pancreatic complications based on timing, and C does not fit the post-pancreatitis upper-abdominal mass pattern.
educational_objective: Recognize persistent upper-abdominal pain with a new palpable mass several weeks after pancreatitis as a pattern that warrants evaluation for a pancreatic pseudocyst or other pancreatic fluid collection.
source_locator: Introduction: pseudocysts are encapsulated pancreatic fluid collections usually maturing more than 4 weeks after pancreatitis. History and Physical: recent pancreatitis plus persistent abdominal pain or new palpable abdominal mass should raise suspicion. Evaluation: CT is a principal imaging modality for pancreatic fluid collections and further evaluation is required for persistent/new symptoms.
source_claim_supported: Several weeks after pancreatitis, persistent abdominal pain with a new palpable abdominal mass is compatible with pancreatic pseudocyst/pancreatic fluid collection and warrants further evaluation.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation: recognize complications of acute illness, identify unexpected findings after treatment/recovery, and intervene for evolving gastrointestinal/pancreatic complications.

source_original.stem: Several weeks after acute pancreatitis, a client has persistent upper-abdominal pain and a newly palpable abdominal mass. Which complication should the nurse suspect?

options.A: Uncomplicated resolution of pancreatitis, because a new palpable abdominal mass is expected during recovery.
options.B: Renal colic, because a pancreatic complication would not persist for several weeks after acute pancreatitis.
options.C: Acute appendicitis, because post-pancreatitis fluid collections do not cause persistent upper-abdominal pain.
options.D: A pancreatic pseudocyst or other post-pancreatitis pancreatic fluid collection requiring further evaluation.

source_original.rationale: Pancreatic fluid collections, including pseudocysts, are recognized complications of pancreatitis. Persistent pain and a new abdominal mass after pancreatitis warrant further clinical evaluation rather than being assumed to represent routine recovery.
source_original.source_detail: Clinical presentation and evaluation of pancreatic pseudocyst after pancreatitis, including persistent abdominal symptoms and mass effect. StatPearls update 2026-04-15; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: acute/complex alterations, emergency response and pathophysiologic adaptation. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the post-pancreatitis fluid-collection construct and key D, tightened the timing to the source-supported several-weeks/>4-week pseudocyst context, clarified that the finding warrants evaluation rather than definitive diagnosis, and reduced difficulty from hard to medium.

audit_findings.currentness: StatPearls Pancreatic Pseudocyst updated 2026-04-15 and live-rechecked 2026-08-16
audit_findings.exact_locator: Introduction; History and Physical; Evaluation sections
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item asks which complication should be suspected/evaluated and does not diagnose a pseudocyst solely from a palpable mass without imaging.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because a new mass with persistent pain is not an expected uncomplicated recovery finding.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because pseudocysts specifically develop/mature after pancreatitis over subsequent weeks.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because the location/timing and post-pancreatitis context favor a pancreatic complication rather than appendicitis.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only D integrates the pancreatitis history, delayed timing, persistent upper-abdominal pain and new mass without overclaiming definitive imaging diagnosis.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are clinical interpretations of the same post-pancreatitis presentation.
audit_findings.blueprint: Physiological Adaptation — recognition of delayed complications after acute pancreatitis.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked the April 2026 StatPearls pseudocyst update, symptom/timing/evaluation sections, all alternatives, rationale, objective, ambiguity, cueing and NCSBN mapping. D remained uniquely correct.
